How this guide is organized Built from Dr. Paul Nash's Immunologic Disorders of the Kidney (slides + narration). He frames five diseases by which arm of the immune system does the damage: type II (antibody on a fixed antigen), type III (immune complexes), or type IV (T cells). Practice questions sit at the end of the section they test. The in-depth summary table is the last section. beyond source marks standard teaching points I added; corrected marks places where the source needed fixing.

1. Roadmap: Five Diseases, Three Mechanisms

DiseaseHypersensitivityAntigenAutoimmune?IF pattern
GoodpastureType IIBasement membrane (fixed in place; kidney + lung)YesLinear
SLE nephritisType IIINuclear/cellular antigens (DNA + DNA-associated proteins)YesGranular
IgA nephropathy (Berger)Type IIIAbnormally modified patient IgAYesGranular (IgA + C3)
Post-strep GNType IIIStreptococcal antigens (foreign)NoGranular
Acute interstitial nephritisType IVDrug/infection antigensNo (drug/infection driven)Negative
The one-line logicAntibody stuck on the basement membrane = linear. Antibody-antigen complexes that lodge in capillaries = granular. T-cell disease = little or no antibody on IF.
Dr. Nash's learning objectivesExplain pathogenesis and general features of Goodpasture, SLE, IgA nephropathy, PSGN and AIN, and differentiate Goodpasture, SLE, IgAN and PSGN (the slide-30 table is the core of that).

2. Immunology Review

Antibody isotypes

IgG, IgM, IgD, IgA, IgE. Janeway/Garland Science, from Dr. Nash's slides.
  • IgG: most common antibody in blood and tissue; relevant to every disorder in this lecture; can fix complement.
  • IgM: also fixes complement but is less common in these kidney diseases; always a pentamer in circulation.
  • IgA: monomer or dimer in blood. Its famous job is secretory antibody across mucosa, but here it's the circulating IgA that matters (IgA nephropathy).
  • IgD and IgE: not involved in any of these kidney diseases.
Dimeric IgA and pentameric IgM (both with J chain).

Complement

Lectin, classical and alternative pathways converge on C3 convertase. Janeway's Immunobiology.
  • Three pathways exist. The classical pathway (started by IgG or IgM bound to antigen) is the one behind the kidney disease here.
  • Three outcomes: inflammation (vasodilation, immune-cell recruitment, increased vascular permeability), opsonization (phagocytes activated; collateral damage), and lysis of cells.
  • C3 is "used up" when complement is being consumed by deposits, so serum C3 can fall. That is why C3 is a diagnostic clue (Section 9).

Hypersensitivity types in play

Four hypersensitivity categories. Janeway's Immunobiology, 8th ed.
TypeEffectorAntigenKidney damage
IIAntibody (not IgE; usually IgG)Fixed on a cell surface or extracellular matrixComplement activation → inflammation, lysis, neutrophil activation (incl. NETosis)
IIIIgG/IgMFree-floating ("soluble," though not strictly true in every case)Complexes lodge in small capillaries → complement → endothelial/tissue damage
IVT cellsCell/tissue-bound or drug-modifiedTh1 (macrophage recruitment), Th2 (eosinophils), Th17 (usually travels with Th1), CTL (direct killing)
Type II: antibody on a cell/matrix activates complement; Fc receptors and complement by-products (C5a, C3a) activate leukocytes → inflammation and tissue injury.

Type II can also act through receptor binding (antibody blocks or mimics the normal signal), but in renal pathology, complement activation is what matters.

Why immune complexes hit the kidney: size and ratio

Immune-complex size depends on the antibody : antigen ratio. The Immune System, 3rd ed.
StageRatioComplexesResult
EarlyAntigen excessSmall; antibodies saturatedUsually not a problem (don't fix complement well, aren't cleared)
IntermediateEquivalenceLarge latticesFix complement, clear from circulation, damage can occur
LateAntibody excessSmall; antigens saturatedUsually not a problem
Complexes deposited in a vessel wall: complement activation, neutrophil recruitment, fibrin and thrombus. Elsevier 2018.
  • Damage is worst in small capillaries or where flow is limited. Glomerular capillaries are tiny, so the kidney is a prime site for type III disease.
  • Complexes get stuck; complement acts locally, causing some blockage and damage to endothelium and underlying cells.
Don't mix these upType II = antibody against a fixed target (basement membrane). Type III = antibody against a free antigen, forming complexes that deposit. Both use complement; the IF pattern is how you tell them apart.

3. Reference Points: Normal Glomerulus and Reading IF

Normal glomerulus by light microscopy: thin delicate capillary loops, normal endothelial and mesangial cell numbers, normal surrounding tubules.

What each biopsy tool shows

ToolWhat you seeUsed in this lecture for
Light microscopyCell number, capillary loop shape, inflammatory infiltratesDamaged glomeruli, immune cells (e.g., neutrophils in PSGN)
Immunofluorescence (IF)Fluorescent anti-antibody (and anti-C3) painted onto the biopsy shows where antibody is sittingLinear vs granular vs negative
Electron microscopy (EM)Dense deposits within or on the basement membraneImmune-complex deposits in SLE
IF in one breathFluorescent-tagged antibodies specific for other antibodies are added to the biopsy and viewed under a UV microscope, so you see the location of the patient's antibodies. Linear = narrow, clear lines along the basement membrane. Granular = random clumps.
Dr. Nash's noteHe leaves detailed histology to the histologists; he points out only the pathology that reflects unwanted immune activity.

4. Goodpasture Syndrome (Anti-GBM Disease)

Basement-membrane antigens → APC → T and B cells → anti-basement membrane antibody → glomerulonephritis + alveolar hemorrhage.

Pathogenesis

  • The mediator is antibody against the basement membrane. Exactly how tolerance breaks isn't clear: basement-membrane antigen somehow reaches antigen-presenting cells in a form they recognize, so the specific immune response begins and antibodies are made.
  • Autoimmune (self antigen) and type II hypersensitivity (fixed antigen; antibody is not IgE).
  • Antibody binds the basement membrane in the kidney and lungs. Complement activation + direct attack → inflammation and damage.

Biopsy

Left column: Goodpasture (abnormal glomerulus on top; linear IF below). Right column: lupus (granular IF). Elsevier 2018.
  • Light microscopy shows distinct morphologic abnormalities compared with the normal glomerulus.
  • IF is linear: because antibody binds the basement membrane directly, it paints a narrow, clear line wherever basement membrane exists.
  • ANA negative; no IgA deposition. Slide 30 leaves the C3 box blank for Goodpasture.
Correction correctedIn the answer to Question B, the transcript says linear IgG (Goodpasture) "would show low serum complement." The deck's own diagnostic table leaves C3 blank for Goodpasture, and in practice serum C3/C4 are typically normal in anti-GBM disease (the complement is consumed locally on the membrane). Don't use low C3 to separate Goodpasture from the others; use linear IF.

Boards extras beyond source

  • Target = the α3 chain of type IV collagen (non-collagenous domain) in the GBM and alveolar basement membrane.
  • Classic picture: hemoptysis + hematuria/rapidly progressive GN (crescents on biopsy); young men and a second peak in older adults; often smokers or after a lung insult.
  • Treatment: plasmapheresis (removes antibody) plus steroids and cyclophosphamide.

5. Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) Nephritis

Characteristic facial (malar) rash. "Lupus" = wolf; the rash was thought to look like a wolf bite.
A: autoantibody production → immune complexes, complement fixation, glomerulonephritis. B: autoantigen presentation to T cells. C: inflammatory cytokines.

Pathogenesis

  • SLE has many manifestations. The kidney injury here is indirect, from antigen-antibody complexes: an autoimmune type III hypersensitivity.
  • Autoantibodies against cellular components, including nuclear antigens. Antigens released from damaged cells are bound by antibody and form complexes.
  • Complexes lodge in small kidney capillaries; antibody activates complement; local damage follows. The same complexes cause the rash and lung damage.
  • The "anti-DNA" antibodies are really directed at DNA-associated proteins and other nuclear antigens (his clarification).

Biopsy

Left: glomerular damage with immune cell infiltrate. Middle: granular IF. Right: electron micrograph with immune-complex deposits ("granular deposits of immunoglobulin and complement in the basement membrane").
  • Light microscopy: glomerular damage and inflammatory infiltrate. EM: visible immune-complex deposits.
  • IF: granular, random clumped deposition (versus the clean line of Goodpasture).
  • Low C3 (consumed by complement activation).

The ANA test

Slide of cells (antigen) → patient serum (primary antibody) → fluorescent anti-human antibody (secondary).
Bound ANA lights up cell nuclei (green). Different patterns occur in different diseases.
  1. A slide coated with human cells provides the antigen.
  2. Add the patient's serum. Any antibody that recognizes the antigens binds.
  3. Add a fluorescent anti-human antibody to tag the bound patient antibody; view under UV.
  4. Positive = nuclear staining. A positive ANA is often associated with lupus and helps separate SLE from the other nephropathies.
Don't confuseThe ANA is a blood test on serum using cells on a slide. It is not performed on the kidney biopsy.

Boards extras beyond source

  • ANA is sensitive but not specific. Anti-dsDNA and anti-Smith are the specific antibodies; anti-dsDNA titer tracks lupus nephritis activity.
  • Low C3 and C4 (classical pathway consumption) support active nephritis.
  • Most dangerous histology: ISN/RPS class IV (diffuse proliferative) with subendothelial deposits, "wire-loop" capillaries, and a "full-house" IF (IgG, IgA, IgM, C3, C1q). Class V is membranous (nephrotic).

6. IgA Nephropathy (Berger Disease)

Mucosal B-cell activation → polymeric galactose-deficient IgA1 → anti-IgA1 IgG autoantibody → circulating immune complex → glomerular deposition (mesangial IgA) → complement activation.

Pathogenesis

  • Another immune-complex (type III) disease, and also autoimmune: the antigen is the patient's own IgA.
  • Prevailing hypothesis: the patient's IgA is abnormally glycosylated. That changes its epitopes so the immune system sees it as abnormal or foreign, and IgG is made against the IgA.
  • As in lupus, antigen-antibody complexes deposit in the kidney and activated complement causes damage.
Wording fix correctedThe slide says the modified IgA "contains galactose," and the transcript says it "does contain galactose." The established finding is the opposite: it is galactose-deficient IgA1 (the O-linked hinge glycans lack galactose, exposing new epitopes), as the deck's own figure labels it. Remember it as "galactose-deficient IgA1 → anti-IgA IgG → complexes."

Biopsy

IF for IgA (left) and C3 (right): both show deposits.
  • IF is granular (like SLE). IgA deposition is diagnostic. C3 deposition can also be seen.
  • Serum C3 is normal (slide 30), unlike SLE and PSGN. ANA negative.

Boards extras beyond source

  • Typical: recurrent gross hematuria 1–3 days after a mucosal (URI or GI) infection ("synpharyngitic"), often in a young adult. Compare PSGN, which lags the infection by 1–3 weeks.
  • Mucosal infection → more IgA made → more target antigen (the logic in his Question B answer).
  • Deposits sit in the mesangium. Related to Henoch-Schönlein purpura (IgA vasculitis). Most common primary GN worldwide. Many cases are mild; some progress to CKD.

7. Post-Streptococcal Glomerulonephritis (PSGN)

Strep pharyngitis → strep antigens → antibodies → glomerular Ab-Ag complexes + complement activation (↓ C3, subepithelial humps) → neutrophils degranulate → hypercellular glomeruli, capillary collapse, ↓ GFR, ↑ creatinine, hematuria (dark urine).

Pathogenesis

  • Follows infection with Streptococcus, primarily S. pyogenes: usually pharyngitis, but also scarlet fever or other strep infections.
  • Type III: complexes of circulating strep antigens + antibodies (made while fighting the infection). Because the antigen is foreign, this is NOT autoimmune.
  • Injury comes from inflammation, directly and indirectly, and from NETosis by recruited neutrophils.

Biopsy

Normal glomerulus (left); light microscopy with increased inflammatory cells (neutrophils) (middle); IF with immune-complex deposits in capillary walls (right).
  • Light microscopy: neutrophils infiltrate the glomerulus, with other damage.
  • IF with antibody against strep antigens shows granular clumps, like the other immune-complex diseases.
  • Low C3; ANA negative; recent strep infection / anti-strep antibody is the key diagnostic factor.

Boards extras beyond source

  • Nephritic syndrome 1–3 weeks after pharyngitis (about 6 weeks after skin infection): hematuria (cola-colored urine), RBC casts, hypertension, periorbital edema, mild proteinuria.
  • Labs: ↑ ASO and anti-DNase B (the flow chart's "incr ASO"); low C3 that recovers in about 8–12 weeks.
  • EM: subepithelial "humps"; IF: "starry sky"/lumpy-bumpy. Children usually recover with supportive care.

8. Acute Interstitial Nephritis (AIN)

AIN summary slide: etiologies, signs, urine findings, histopathology, treatment.

Mechanism

  • Type IV hypersensitivity, T-cell mediated. Sometimes Th1, sometimes CD8 cytotoxic cells, occasionally Th2; Th17 may be mixed in.
  • Most common cause: drugs (legal or illegal). Mechanisms: the drug binds a protein and creates a new epitope, molecular mimicry, or others. Infections and autoimmune disease can also be involved.
  • Onset is delayed after the drug or infection starts because the response has to develop (referring to first exposure).
  • Cytokines: IFN-γ, IL-2, IL-17, TNF drive most inflammation and recruit immune cells.
  • Result: interstitial edema, tubular atrophy, and eventually fibrosis and chronic disease.

Findings and treatment

FeatureDetail
Etiologies (figure)Drugs: NSAIDs, beta-lactams, diuretics, PPIs, anti-cancer drugs. Infections: Legionella, CMV, Streptococcus. Other: sarcoidosis, SLE.
SignsRash, fever, eosinophilia
UrineSterile pyuria, eosinophiluria, WBC casts, proteinuria
HistologyInterstitial edema with WBC infiltration; possible granulomas; chronic: fibrosis, scarring, atrophy
IFNegative / little antibody; no antibody in complexes, to basement membrane, or to nuclear antigens
C3Normal (no consumption)
TreatmentStop the drug / treat the infection
The AIN tellA biopsy with negligible IgG, IgA and C3 points to AIN: every other disease in this lecture involves antibody that IF would detect.

Boards extras beyond source

  • Unlike the glomerulonephritides, AIN is a tubulointerstitial process: expect a rising creatinine and pyuria/WBC casts rather than a nephritic picture with RBC casts. The full rash-fever-eosinophilia triad is present in a minority.
  • If stopping the drug isn't enough, corticosteroids are commonly used.
  • Look at the med list: new NSAID, PPI, antibiotic (penicillins, cephalosporins, sulfonamides) days to weeks earlier.

9. Differentiating the Five Diseases

Dr. Nash's diagnostics table (slide 30)

DiseaseIFC3Recent strep / anti-strep AbANAIgA deposition (IFA)
SLEGranularLowPositiveNo
GoodpastureLinearNegativeNo
IgA nephropathyGranularNormalNegativeYes
Post-strepGranularLowYesNegativeNo
AINNegativeNormalNegativeNo

Blank cells are blank on his slide. He says this is not a comprehensive differential, just useful distinguishing characteristics.

A four-step approach

  1. IF pattern first: linear → Goodpasture. Negative → AIN (T-cell). Granular → one of the three immune-complex diseases.
  2. Among granular: IgA deposition → IgA nephropathy.
  3. Of the remaining two (both with low C3): positive ANA → SLE.
  4. Recent strep infection / anti-strep antibody (and ANA negative) → PSGN.
Side-by-side IFGoodpasture (left) = clear, narrow, basement-membrane lines. Lupus (right) = random, clumped granular deposits. See the figure in Section 4.

Quick contrasts

  • Antibody ON the membrane (type II) vs complexes lodged IN the capillaries (type III) = linear vs granular.
  • Autoimmune: Goodpasture, SLE, IgAN. Not autoimmune: PSGN (foreign strep antigen) and AIN (T-cell response to drug/infection).
  • Low C3: SLE and PSGN (his table). Normal C3: IgAN and AIN.
  • NETosis is highlighted for type II (Goodpasture) and PSGN.

10. Dr. Nash's Main Points

DiseaseHis summary
GoodpastureType II autoimmune disease; antibodies attack the basement membrane (kidney and lungs); complement activation → inflammation and kidney damage; antibody along the membrane → linear IF.
SLEType III autoimmune; antibodies to DNA (really DNA-associated proteins) and other antigens form complexes that lodge in kidneys and elsewhere; granular deposits on EM or IF; complement → inflammation; ANA positive (patient serum + fluorescent anti-human secondary on human cells; nuclear binding).
IgA nephropathyType III autoimmunity: antibodies against modified IgA; IgG specific for IgA forms complexes that lodge in the kidney; complement → inflammation; granular IF like SLE; IgA deposition is diagnostic; C3 can be seen.
PSGNAntibodies against Streptococcus (usually S. pyogenes) form complexes with bacterial antigens deposited in the kidney during infection and persisting afterward; history of strep throat or other infection; damage from complement inflammation and NETosis.
AINType IV hypersensitivity to drug or infection antigens; Th1, CD8, rarely Th2, plus Th17; CD8 cytotoxicity or inflammation damages the kidney; IFN-γ, IL-2, IL-17, TNF; chronic disease can develop; limited antibody involvement, so tests show negligible antibody.

Mechanism and cell summary

ConceptRemember
IsotypesIgG most common and relevant to all; IgG/IgM fix complement (classical pathway); IgM pentamer; IgA monomer/dimer (circulating IgA matters in IgAN); IgD/IgE not involved.
ComplementInflammation, opsonization, lysis. C3 consumed in SLE and PSGN.
Type II vs IIIFixed antigen (membrane) vs free antigen (complexes). Both: complement + neutrophils (NETosis).
Immune complex ratioLarge, damaging complexes form near equivalence; antigen excess or antibody excess gives small, harmless complexes.
Why kidneyTiny glomerular capillaries trap complexes; complement acts locally.
Type IVTh1, Th2, Th17, CTL. AIN = T-cell; IFN-γ, IL-2, IL-17, TNF.
